subtype: Email that says too little or too much [Actor]
passage: Gargi typed the email to her manager Hafsa in a rush, because the flight was due to board in half an hour. It ran nine paragraphs: the college project, the survey she had planned, three problems with the form, an apology, and only at the very end, "Could I have access to the customer list by Friday?" Hafsa, standing in the airport queue with one bar of signal, skimmed the first two lines and put the phone away. No reply came. Gargi waited two hours and then rewrote it: subject "Need customer list access by Friday", the first line asking for exactly that, two lines of reason. She sent it. From the gate Hafsa replied: "Approved. Sending link."

qa.q: Where was the request in Gargi's first email?
qa.a: It was at the very end, after nine paragraphs.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as she typed the first email in a rush?
qa.a: Hurried and anxious, packing in every detail and apology.

qa.q: What did Gargi change in the rewrite?
qa.a: A clear subject line, the request in the first line and just two lines of reason.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa put the phone away after two lines?
qa.a: Hafsa was in a queue with weak signal and could not see what was needed, so skimmed and set it aside.

grounding: Shows an intern burying the ask at the end of a long email and then putting the purpose and action in the first lines.

passage: Irawati's email to the department coordinator, Siddharth, said only: "Sir, regarding the form. Please check. Thanks." She pressed send and felt done. Two days later there was no reply. She met Siddharth in the corridor, and he said, "Which form? Check what? I get sixty emails a day." Her cheeks burned. That night she wrote again. Subject: "Internship form: signature needed by 12 October." First line: "Could you please sign the attached internship form by 12 October?" Then two lines on why. Siddharth replied the next afternoon: "Signed. Collect it from the office."

qa.q: What did Irawati's first email say?
qa.a: It said: "Sir, regarding the form. Please check. Thanks."

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when the coordinator asked "Which form? Check what?"
qa.a: Embarrassed, since her cheeks burned.

qa.q: What change to the second email made it work?
qa.a: A specific subject line, the request in the first line and a deadline date.

qa.q: How does Siddharth's inbox explain the missing reply?
qa.a: He gets sixty emails a day, so a vague message with no clear request is hard to act on and easy to skip.

grounding: Shows a student sending an email with no clear request and then rewriting it with the purpose and action up front.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Three days, no reply from Suraj. I finally asked him at lunch. He looked puzzled. "Your email? I saw it was long. I was going to read it properly this weekend."
It was long. I opened it again tonight. Four paragraphs about the survey, the problems I faced, what I tried, and then, in the very last line: "So could you approve access to the data folder?" The only thing I needed was hiding at the bottom.
I felt my face burn. I'd been waiting three days for a one-click approval.
I wrote a new email. Subject: "Request: access to survey data folder by Thursday." First line: "Could you approve my access to the data folder? I need it to finish the survey report by Friday." Then two short lines of background.
Suraj replied in six minutes: "Done." I'm Tanuja, an intern, and I just learned the most useful thing of this internship.

qa.q: Where was the request in Tanuja's first email?
qa.a: It was in the very last line.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel on rereading the first email?
qa.a: Tanuja felt embarrassed, face burning, at having waited three days for a one-click approval hidden at the bottom.

qa.q: What made the second email work?
qa.a: The request and the deadline came in the subject and the first line, with only two short lines of background.

qa.q: How might Suraj have seen the first email?
qa.a: Suraj saw a long email and put it off for the weekend, not knowing a quick approval was waiting inside it.

grounding: Illustrates an intern whose long email buries the request at the end, and who learns to put the purpose and ask in the first lines.

passage:
In Bhadrak, the cyber café had one slow computer and a fan that squeaked. Mahima, in her second year of college, sat in front of it writing to the university exam office. Her marksheet showed "absent" for a paper she had written.
She typed for twenty minutes: how she had studied, which room she sat in, how her friend had seen her there, how upset her parents were. The actual request came in the last paragraph.
Rafiq, who ran the café, glanced at the screen as he passed. "Mahima, they get hundreds of these. What do you want them to do?"
"Correct my marksheet."
"Then say that first."
She sighed, but she started again. Subject: "Correction request: marked absent in Physics Paper 2, Roll No. 4417." First line: "I was present for this exam; please correct my result." Then the room number, the invigilator's signature on her hall ticket, attached. Five lines. She clicked send.

qa.q: What did Mahima's marksheet show for the paper she had written?
qa.a: Her marksheet showed "absent" for a paper she had written.

qa.q: How was Mahima feeling as she typed the first version?
qa.a: Mahima felt upset and anxious, pouring out her whole story because she was worried the office would not believe her.

qa.q: What small change made Mahima's email stronger?
qa.a: Putting the request and roll number in the subject and first line, then attaching the proof in a few short lines.

qa.q: How might the exam office clerk see the second email?
qa.a: The clerk would likely find it quick to understand and act on, since the request and proof are right at the top.

grounding: Illustrates a student whose long email buries the request, and who rewrites it so the purpose and ask come first.

subtype: Email that says too little or too much [Actor]
passage: On Thursday evening at the Tokyo studio, Yuki sent her supervisor, Kwame, the email she had spent forty minutes on. It began with how the week had gone, the client's feedback on poster colours, a funny story about the printer, a note on the new intern's desk and a long paragraph of ideas for the next campaign. In the fifth paragraph, halfway down, was the one thing she needed: approval by Friday noon to buy the typeface licence, or the print order would slip. Kwame replied at 11 pm: "Great update, thanks Yuki! 👍" Nothing about the licence. On Friday at two, the print shop called to ask where the files were. Yuki's stomach sank. She opened a new email. Subject: Need your OK today: typeface licence. First line: "Can you approve the typeface licence today? Without it, printing slips to Tuesday." Kwame answered in four minutes: "Approved. Sorry, I skimmed."

qa.q: In which paragraph was Yuki's request for approval?
qa.a: In the fifth paragraph.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel when the print shop called on Friday?
qa.a: Her stomach sank; she was dismayed and frustrated that the one request that mattered had been missed.

qa.q: What made the second email work?
qa.a: The request was in the subject and the first line, with the reason and the consequence, so Kwame could act in four minutes.

qa.q: How might Kwame have read the first email?
qa.a: Kwame probably skimmed a long, chatty update late at night, enjoyed it, and never reached the buried request, which Kwame later admits.

grounding: Shows an intern whose long email buries the real request, so the reader skims past it, until the ask moves to the first line.
